<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with clean structure, proper A1/A2 labels, and disciplined use of ordinary background knowledge. PRO built a memorable frame ("rubble or vault"), a strong due-process reason to prefer courts over executive fiat, and a genuinely sharp dilemma: CON's freeze either eventually returns the money to an unrepentant aggressor (insurance) or is a permanent taking without trial. CON, however, did more damaging comparative work. It turned PRO's own centerpiece precedent (the Iraq/Kuwait compensation mechanism was Council-mandated, consent-based and funded by an oil levy, not judicial execution against reserves), supplied a live counter-model (freeze-plus-negotiation, Iran/Algiers) and one empirical observation PRO never fully defused: the very governments custodying frozen reserves immobilize principal and spend only windfall income, which both undercuts PRO's actor question and grounds the systemic-risk story. PRO's clever "interest concedes the principle, only scale is contested" reply was met with a plausible "scale is the principle" distinction between a custody fee and destroying a state's monetary core. CON also answered PRO's endpoint pressure directly (conditioned release, assets outlive regimes, income flows now) rather than dodging. PRO's closing crystallization was excellent, but CON's reversibility framing — a judgment that cannot travel versus a precedent that travels everywhere — left the cleaner decision rule standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's symmetry follow-through: PRO answered the mirror-court worry by saying no third jurisdiction would recognize a hostile aggression judgment, and CON showed the answer collapses because mirror courts need no foreign recognition — the retaliating state's targets (foreign investors' assets) already sit inside its own jurisdiction, so the boomerang operates entirely at home. Coupled with the observation that actual reserve custodians touch only windfall interest, this materially damaged PRO's route.</best_rebuttal>
